h1: Whisky writing and journalism as a career
title: Whisky Writing as a Career | Craft Beer School
desc: How people build a career writing about whisky: the kinds of work, the skills editors want, ethics and responsible coverage in India.
teaser: Whisky writing pays in knowledge before it pays in money. Here is how people build a career from it.
standfirst: Whisky writing covers tasting notes, distillery features, industry news, books, brand copy and education. Few people do it full time. Many build it alongside another job until it grows. Here is what the work involves and what makes a writer worth reading.
sections:
Whisky writing is not one job. It includes:

  • Reviews and tasting notes for magazines, websites and newsletters.
  • Features on distilleries, regions and people.
  • Trade journalism on business, regulation and markets.
  • Books and long-form guides.
  • Commissioned copy for brands, retailers and events.
  • Education material for courses and tastings.

Most working writers mix several of these. Editorial work builds a reputation. Commercial work often pays the bills. Keeping the two clearly separate matters for credibility.

Readers can tell when a writer does not understand the subject. A good whisky writer knows how whisky is made, the legal definitions of the main categories and how casks shape flavour. Scotch must mature at least three years in oak in Scotland. Bourbon must use at least 51% corn and new charred oak containers. Small facts like these trip up careless writers.

Indian whisky needs particular care. Much of the market blends neutral spirit with malt spirit, while Indian single malts are made from malted barley and mature fast in the heat. Our guide to Indian single malt explains the distinction.

A tasting note is the basic unit of whisky writing. Good notes are specific, honest and useful. Instead of listing a dozen flavours, they say what stands out and how the whisky changes with water or time in the glass. They note the strength, because a whisky at 46% ABV tastes very different from one at 40%.

Our guide to writing whisky tasting notes covers the craft in detail. Practise by writing notes on the same whisky on different days and comparing them.

Brands send samples, host trips and sponsor events. That is normal in drinks writing, but it creates pressure. Disclose free samples and paid trips to readers. Keep commissioned copy separate from editorial reviews. Never write a review in exchange for payment without saying so.

Independence is a writer's main asset. Once readers suspect a writer is selling, the writing loses its value.

Alcohol advertising is restricted in India. Editorial writing is different from advertising, but writers should still avoid content that reads as promotion, appeals to people under the legal drinking age or links drinking with success or driving. Responsible tasting coverage mentions small measures, water and pacing where it fits. Never suggest drinking and driving is acceptable.

Social media adds extra care. Platforms have their own rules on alcohol content. Age gates matter.

Whisky writing is full of myths repeated from one article to the next. Some are harmless. Others mislead readers. A careful writer checks claims against primary sources: the legal definitions published by governments, the technical literature on distillation and maturation and what a distillery itself states on the record.

Watch out for numbers. Ages, percentages and dates need a source. A claim that a whisky is aged in a particular cask or for a particular time should come from the producer, not from another blog. When you cannot check a fact, leave it out. Editors remember writers who never need correcting.

Visit distilleries where you can. Seeing a pot still run, smelling new make spirit and walking a warehouse gives you details that make writing come alive. It also makes it much harder to repeat a myth, because you have seen the process for yourself.

Keep a notebook of every fact you check and where it came from. Over a few years it becomes your own reference library, faster to search than the internet and far more reliable.

Editors hire writers whose work they have already seen. Start a blog or newsletter and publish regularly. Pitch short pieces to publications with a clear idea, a reason it matters now and why you are the right person to write it. Attend tastings and trade events to meet people. Over time, specialise: a writer known for Indian single malt or for cask science stands out more than a generalist.

Formal training helps. Distilling and sensory courses give writers the vocabulary and credibility that self-study takes years to build.

Pick one whisky style you find interesting and write a thousand words on how it is made, using only sources you can check. Then cut it to five hundred. The difference between the two versions is where your editing skill will grow.
faqs: Can you make a living from whisky writing?
Some do, usually by combining editorial writing, commercial copy, books and education. Many start part time.
Should whisky writers accept free samples?
It is common, but disclose samples and trips to readers and keep paid copy separate from reviews.
Do I need a qualification to write about whisky?
No, but courses in distilling and sensory evaluation build knowledge and credibility quickly.
